extracted.intended_audience: short fiction writers submitting to magazines (science fiction & fantasy)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for authors submitting speculative short fiction to magazines about what editors look for, how to approach submissions, and realistic expectations about feedback and career paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the story you're passionate about
rubrics_metrics.description: "What I really want is the story you're passionate about writing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Surprise me. Take me somewhere I wasn't expecting." Editors appreciate work that reflects the author's passion and originality rather than stories tailored to guess an editor's current whim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't write to guess the editor's current tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Trust me when I say that I don't want the story you think I want. I get bored easily and my interests are a moving target."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trying to second-guess or chase perceived short-term trends for a specific editor; even if you hit it once, tastes move and the payoff is short-lived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep improving your craft (practice makes perfect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors notice authors who "never stopped improving their craft."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continual learning, experimentation, and submission over time matter. Early rejections are common; improvement and persistence increase chances of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and submission history matters
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first time I publish an author, I look back at all the stories they've previously submitted to us. This is more of a test for me."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A track record of repeated submissions and visible improvement can influence editorial decisions; persistence signals seriousness and growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push outside your comfort zone
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pushing outside your comfort zone can be extremely beneficial, even if only as an exercise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with forms, styles, or subjects you wouldn't normally write to develop skills and discover stronger work; short-term exercises can inform longer-term growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-publishing is a viable alternative (with trade-offs)
rubrics_metrics.description: "And yes, it's sometimes viable to just shortcut the process by self-publishing. It comes with its own can of worms, but it's a completely viable path for some."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize self-publishing as an option when traditional routes aren't right, but be aware of the different challenges and responsibilities it entails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect personalized rejections from busy editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections are usually form letters: editors don't provide individualized feedback because of time constraints (e.g., ~1,100 submissions/month would require ~91 extra hours/month for five-minute notes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the practical reasons (workload, response speed) editors prioritize broad activities over individualized critique. Seek feedback through workshops, classes, or slush-reading experience instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors prioritize fast response time over detailed per-submission feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: "We aim to respond to submissions in a day or two... another downside to personalized rejections would be a significant delay in our response time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rapid reply often means less individualized commentary; longer waits may simply reflect time in the slush pile rather than careful critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and learn the market by volunteering as a slush reader
rubrics_metrics.description: "That’s one of the reasons I often encourage authors to consider volunteering as slush readers (not just here, anywhere)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slush reading exposes you to what editors see, helps you gauge originality, and improves submission instincts. Reading broadly reduces the chance of thinking your idea is uniquely new when it isn't.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is no single path to success
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different routes (traditional publication, self-publishing, workshops, contests) can lead to success; choose strategies that fit your goals and keep experimenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value quality over quantity in how editors spend time
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors prefer to allocate time to things that have greater impact (guest instructing, panels, judging) rather than spending short bursts on many individual rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should understand editorial time is finite and that meaningful, time-consuming feedback is often provided in more formal venues (workshops, classes) rather than in routine rejection notes.
